analysis.one_liner: Bars federal and state lawsuits blaming food companies for weight gain, obesity, and related health conditions.
analysis.headline: The bill drew a bipartisan sponsor team and 7 cosponsors but never got a committee or floor vote, dying in a House subcommittee when the 111th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would prohibit any new lawsuit in federal or state court against food manufacturers, sellers, marketers, advertisers, distributors, or their trade associations claiming that a person's eating habits caused weight gain, obesity, or related health problems [S2][S3]. It would also require courts to immediately dismiss any such lawsuits already pending on the day the bill became law [S3]. Only three narrow exceptions would survive: breaches of an express contract or warranty unrelated to weight, claims that a company knowingly broke an advertising or labeling law that someone relied on, and enforcement actions by the FTC or FDA [S2][S3]. The bill never left the House Judiciary Committee, so none of this took effect [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Food and beverage companies, restaurants, advertisers, and their trade associations would gain a federal shield against obesity-related lawsuits. No such case could be filed, and any case pending when the bill passed would be thrown out immediately [S2][S3]. The shield would also apply to trade associations themselves, a group rarely subject to civil suits [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Food and beverage companies and their trade associations

how_it_helps.text: It bans any new civil action, in any court, against food manufacturers, marketers, distributors, advertisers, sellers, or trade associations for injuries tied to accumulated food consumption, weight gain, obesity, or related health conditions [S2][S3].
It requires courts to dismiss, immediately and by operation of law, any covered lawsuit pending on the date of enactment [S3].
It stays discovery (the forced sharing of internal company documents) whenever a defendant files or plans to file a motion claiming the bill applies, except in limited court-ordered cases [S3].
It also covers suits brought by relatives, representatives, or third parties on behalf of the injured person, and any follow-on or derivative claims [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Consumers who believe a food product or its marketing caused them harm would lose their day in court in nearly all cases, and state courts would lose the power to hear these claims under their own laws. The only paths left would be narrow contract or warranty claims unrelated to weight, suits requiring proof of a knowing statutory violation that a person relied on, or government enforcement by the FTC or FDA [S2][S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Consumers seeking to sue over food-related health harm

drawbacks.text: The bill would strip consumers of a legal remedy and displace state court authority, since the ban applies in both federal and state courts and pending state cases would be dismissed by law [S2][S3].

The exceptions are narrow and hard to meet: a consumer would have to show a company knowingly violated a specific marketing, advertising, or labeling statute, that the consumer relied on that violation, and that this reliance was the direct cause of the injury [S3].
Even the excepted claims would be harder to bring, because the bill lets courts freeze discovery whenever a defendant invokes the act, delaying access to internal company records [S3].

The bill's findings declare that weight gain and obesity 'cannot be attributed to the consumption of any specific food or beverage' — a legal conclusion that would preempt juries and judges from weighing the facts in individual cases [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the food industry, the benefit is a broad, permanent liability shield that goes well beyond the few obesity suits actually filed. For consumers, the cost is the loss of nearly all civil remedies, with only narrow exceptions requiring proof of knowing statutory violations — a burden most individuals could rarely meet. Courts were already generally skeptical of obesity-related lawsuits, so the bill's practical effect would be to foreclose even the occasional case with real merit, while moving all policing of food marketing to government agencies.

outcome.mechanism: The House Judiciary Committee referred it to a subcommittee in July 2009, and it never got a markup, a vote, or any further action before the Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: Rep. Dan Boren (D-OK) introduced the bill on February 3, 2009, together with Rep. Pat Tiberi (R-OH) [S1][S3].
The House referred it to the Judiciary Committee the same day, and on July 23, 2009, the committee referred it to the Subcommittee on Commercial and Administrative Law [S5].
No further action was taken — no subcommittee vote, no committee markup, no floor vote — and the bill died when the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011 [S1][S5].
The bill had 7 cosponsors: 6 of 178 House Republicans and 1 of 253 House Democrats [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary consumers and state courts are better off because the bill died: the legal right to sue food companies over weight-related harm remains available, and no pending cases were dismissed. Food and beverage companies did not get the liability shield they sought.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Consumers, who kept their right to sue

for.name: Dan Boren
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the House on February 3, 2009

for.name: Pat Tiberi
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill as its original cosponsor at introduction

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over civil liability law
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a markup or a vote; referred it to the Subcommittee on Commercial and Administrative Law in July 2009 and took no further action

sides.party_line_note: The bill was sponsored by a Democrat with an original Republican cosponsor, and its 7 cosponsors split 6 Republicans to 1 Democrat; no vote ever occurred to reveal a sharper partisan split.

industries.industry: Food and beverage manufacturers and sellers
industries.note: The bill would give these companies a permanent federal shield against weight- and obesity-related lawsuits and require dismissal of any pending ones. Their gain would come directly out of consumers' access to the courts.

industries.industry: Food marketers, advertisers, distributors, and trade associations
industries.note: Marketers, advertisers, distributors, and food trade associations are all named as protected parties, so groups representing the industry would be shielded alongside the companies themselves. This would foreclose claims aimed at advertising practices unless they met the bill's narrow knowing-violation exception.
